vignette:
Leilani was sixty-five years old, a widow of eight years, and a cybersecurity analyst who had spent three decades building firewalls against digital threats. She never imagined the threat would come from inside her own body. The event happened on a Tuesday morning, on a two-lane road she had driven a thousand times. She was on her way to a client site, coffee in the cup holder, her mind already running through packet logs. A driver crossed the center line at sixty miles per hour. Leilani swerved, but not fast enough. The impact spun her car into a drainage ditch, and for a long moment she was suspended upside down, held by her seatbelt, the smell of gasoline and overheated metal filling the cabin. She could feel the wet earth against her right arm where the window had shattered, and a searing pain in her ribs where the steering column had buckled inward. She hung there, unable to move, waiting for the fire she was certain would come. It took the rescue crew twenty minutes to cut her out. She did not lose consciousness, not once. She remembered every second of those twenty minutes—the pressure of the belt against her collarbone, the way the light shifted as clouds passed overhead, the sound of her own breathing, too fast and too shallow, and that smell, that thick sweet smell of fuel and torn metal that she could still summon at will, as if it were stored in a jar on a shelf in her mind.

In the weeks after the accident, Leilani tried to do what she had always done: analyze the problem, contain the breach, move on. She went back to work within ten days, her ribs still taped, her arm in a sling. She told herself that the best way to handle it was to not handle it at all. She avoided anything that might stir up a feeling—no sad movies, no happy ones either, no music with lyrics, no conversations that drifted toward the personal. When colleagues asked how she was, she said “fine” and changed the subject to threat vectors. She found herself replaying the accident in her mind, not the parts she wanted to understand but the same loop: why her, why that road, why that Tuesday. She would lie in bed at night and go over it, searching for a reason that made the randomness bearable, but she never found one. The injustice of it lodged in her chest like a splinter. She had done everything right. She had been sober, alert, within the speed limit, hands at ten and two. And still, a stranger had nearly killed her, and as far as she knew, he had walked away with nothing more than a citation. Nothing had been done. No one had answered for it.

Sleep became a problem almost immediately, but Leilani did not call it insomnia. She called it vigilance. She found it nearly impossible to fall asleep because her body refused to surrender awareness. Every creak of the house, every distant car, every shift of wind against the window—her eyes would snap open, her heart already racing, her hands checking the locks she had checked three times already. She felt safer during the day, when the world was bright and full of witnesses. At night, the darkness felt like a blanket that could hide anything. She would wake at two, three, four in the morning, not from a nightmare but from a sudden, urgent need to confirm that no one was in the room, that the door was still locked, that she was still alive. She would get up, walk the perimeter of her small house, check every window, then lie back down and do it all again an hour later.

The memories came as images more than stories. She could see the grille of the other car growing in her windshield, the exact shade of blue of the sky above the ditch, the pattern of cracks in her own side window as it spiderwebbed inward. But the worst was the physical memory. When she thought about the accident, her ribs would ache, a deep, dull pain exactly where the steering column had struck her. Her right arm would throb as if the glass were still cutting. She knew it was memory, not injury—the doctors had cleared her, the scans were clean—but knowing that did not stop the pain from arriving on schedule. She had come to believe that her body was no longer something she could trust. It had betrayed her, first by being fragile enough to break, and then by refusing to let her forget. She was certain, too, that other people could see it. When she walked into a meeting at work, she felt as though her trauma was written on her skin, that her colleagues could look at her and know exactly what had happened, could see her hanging upside down in that car. She kept her head down, avoided eye contact, and spoke only when spoken to.

She tried to erase the memory entirely. She deleted every photo from that week, threw away the clothes she had been wearing, repainted the room where she had recovered. But the memory was not stored in objects. It was stored in her ribs, in her nose, in the dark hours of the night. The avoidance took a toll. She stopped accepting evening shifts, then stopped attending team dinners, then stopped answering calls from her daughter, who lived three states away and had no idea that her mother had been in an accident at all. Leilani did not want to explain it. She did not want to feel it. She wanted the whole thing to have never happened.

What finally brought her to seek help was not the pain or the sleeplessness or the isolation. It was the moment she realized she could not remember what her husband’s voice sounded like anymore. She had been trying, deliberately, to call up the sound of him saying her name, and there was nothing but static. She had spent so long erasing the bad memories that she had erased the good ones too. She came to the clinic because she was afraid of what she was becoming, and because somewhere underneath the fear, she was hoping that it was not too late to find her way back.
